project.title: Release eval - Brackenridge graded foam filters

sections.s242:
The team did not know whether shrinkage mismatch would tear a part that combines coarse and fine filtration in one ceramic body apart at the interface. The company makes foam-ceramic filters for metal foundries at its plant in Dunmore Falls, Ontario, and set out to build a filter for aluminium foundries that cracks less in the pour and captures more fine inclusions. The team calls the graded structure the cascade-fired lattice. The process lead has six years at the company and earlier worked at a refractory brick maker, so firing curves and shrinkage are familiar ground.

Standard practice falls short because the knowledge needed to combine coarse and fine filtration in one ceramic body did not exist. Stacking filters doubles the cost and leaves a gap between the two pieces where metal can bypass. Thicker fine filters raise thermal stress and make priming harder. Published graded ceramic foam work was mostly lab-scale discs made by gel casting or freeze casting, and no work was found on a replicated foam with a pore gradient through a 50 mm part fired at production scale. Interface stress could not be modelled well because the struts are hollow after burnout.

The technological objective was to advance understanding of firing shrinkage compatibility, fine-inclusion capture versus flow, and thermal shock behaviour at the interface of sponge-replicated ceramic foams with a pore gradient, to create a graded alumina filter with a coarse entry face and a fine exit layer.

Different pore sizes pick up different amounts of slurry, so the zones shrink differently in firing. The team did not know whether shrinkage mismatch would tear the part apart at the interface during firing. Data existed for uniform filters, but not for a part where slurry mass per volume changes across 50 mm. It was also uncertain whether the gradient could raise capture of 20 to 80 micron inclusions while keeping flow and priming head near the standard 20 ppi filter, and whether the graded interface would stop or start cracks under thermal shock, since the literature goes both ways depending on the material.
sections.s244:
The team started from the unresolved question of whether shrinkage mismatch would tear a part with a pore gradient apart at the interface during firing. To test whether different pore sizes pick up different slurry amounts, the team measured slurry pick-up per volume in each zone. The plan was laid out in August 2025; Trial 1 ran in September 2025. It followed a planned order: make graded green bodies that survive firing, test flow and capture on the survivors, then test thermal shock and burst behaviour. Each trial changed one main variable so results could be traced to a cause. One dedicated technician and the process lead at roughly half time did the work.

It was hypothesized that if a two-zone template (10 ppi entry, 30 ppi exit) is coated so both zones carry similar slurry mass per volume, then linear firing shrinkage across the interface will match within 0.5 percent. The part should then survive firing without delamination. It should also capture at least 30 percent more fine inclusions than the standard 20 ppi filter. Flow rate should be no more than 10 percent lower. The team tested this by measuring slurry pick-up and linear firing shrinkage on each zone across the interface.

Trial 1 bonded 10 ppi and 30 ppi sheets (25 mm each) with polyurethane adhesive, coated 24 filters in standard alumina slurry, and fired them on the standard curve. Eighteen of 24 parts delaminated at the bond line. On the survivors the 30 ppi side shrank 1.4 percent more than the 10 ppi side, and the adhesive left a 0.3 to 0.6 mm burnout gap. Pore-size-dependent pick-up drives the mismatch, and the adhesive burns out before the ceramic sinters, so it could not hold the interface.

Trial 2 replaced adhesive with thermally fused templates and used a two-stage dip: the whole part in slurry at about 1,500 mPa.s, then only the coarse half at about 2,400 mPa.s. Pick-up evened to 0.24 g/cm3 on the fine side against 0.22 g/cm3 on the coarse side. Even so, 9 of 40 parts delaminated. Mismatch fell to 0.7 percent, still not good enough for production. The remaining difference pointed to the firing curve.

Trial 3 kept the two-stage dip and added a 1 C/min ramp between 1,100 and 1,350 C and a 45 minute hold at 1,350 C. Of 36 parts, 2 delaminated, and mismatch fell to 0.4 percent, within the 0.5 percent target. The slow ramp added about 3 hours of kiln time per load. Mismatch therefore tracks slurry mass per volume more than pore size, and a slower ramp through the sintering window takes up the remaining difference.

Trial 4 poured 50 kg of A356 at 720 C, six pours each through standard 20 ppi, standard 30 ppi and graded filters. The 20 ppi filter flowed at about 4.1 kg/s. The 30 ppi filter flowed at 2.9 kg/s and needed a 30 percent higher priming head. The graded filter flowed at 3.8 kg/s, 7 percent below the 20 ppi, and captured 41 percent more 20 to 80 micron inclusions. The fine side choked near the end in 2 of 6 pours. Trial 5 cut the fine exit layer from 25 mm to 15 mm. Flow held at 3.9 kg/s across the full 50 kg with no choking, and capture was 36 percent above the 20 ppi filter.

Trial 6 examined thermal shock. In quench tests (700 C into room-temperature water, then crush testing) the standard filter kept about 55 percent of its strength and the graded filter kept 68 percent. In burst tests on 20 filters each, 3 standard filters cracked, while 1 graded filter cracked and the crack stopped at the interface. Of 10 retained Trial 2 parts, 4 cracked along the interface. A well-matched interface therefore arrests cracks, while a poorly matched one becomes the failure plane.
sections.s246:
The team did not know whether shrinkage mismatch would tear a part with a pore gradient apart at the interface. Trial 3 showed it need not. Mismatch was 0.4 percent against the 0.5 percent target, with 2 of 36 parts delaminated. The objective, to advance understanding of firing shrinkage compatibility in sponge-replicated foams with a pore gradient, was partly achieved. The hypothesis was proven for firing survival. Capture and flow were tested in Trials 4 and 5 at 50 mm, so those results remain partial.

It was determined that shrinkage mismatch tracks slurry mass per volume more than pore size. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether different pore sizes would shrink too differently to survive firing. Different pore sizes pick up different amounts of slurry, so the zones shrink differently in firing. Data existed for uniform filters, but not for a part where loading changes across 50 mm. Based on this understanding, the two-stage dip evened pick-up to 0.24 g/cm3 on the fine side against 0.22 g/cm3 on the coarse side. With thermal fusion, Trial 2 cut delamination to 9 of 40 parts. Mismatch of 0.7 percent was still not good enough for production, so Trial 3 added a slower ramp through the sintering window.

Open items for fiscal 2027 include grading at 30 mm total thickness, the highest volume format. It remains uncertain whether the same mismatch control holds there, because pick-up and shrinkage were characterized only across 50 mm. Continuous gradients and a binder change to shorten the slow ramp, which adds about 3 hours of kiln time per load, are also unresolved. The team plans to repeat the firing and flow trials at 30 mm.

The project aimed at a filter that cracks less and captures more fine inclusions. The team did not know if shrinkage mismatch would split the interface, and the work showed that it tracks slurry mass per volume. Trial 3 gave survival through firing, and Trial 5 chose a 15 mm fine exit layer as the better trade.

sections.s242:
Slow nitrification start-up in cold water was the uncertainty that drove this project: it was unknown how to shorten start-up below 10 C in biofilm-heavy recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) water. The company designs recirculating aquaculture systems for land-based trout farms, including tanks, biofilters, oxygen systems and controls. It set out to make its cold-water biofilters start up faster. Clients run cold water, often 6 to 12 C, and the biological systems and controls groups have direct experience of how biofilters behave in these conditions.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to speed nitrification start-up below 10 C was insufficient. Standard start-up is to dose ammonium chloride and wait, or to seed with media from an existing biofilter. Start-up took 9 to 10 weeks below 10 C, versus 3 to 4 weeks at 20 C. Published work and the company's experience indicated that seed media from a warm system goes into shock in 8 C water, where the bacteria survive but barely grow. No documented method was known for preparing seed media to grow at these temperatures.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of cold-water (below 10 C) nitrification start-up, for the purpose of improving the design of RAS biofilters so that start-up takes under 5 weeks at 8 C.

It was uncertain whether stepwise acclimation of seed media, lowering temperature 1 C every 4 days from 14 to 8 C, could shorten nitrification start-up at 8 C. Warm seed media goes into shock at that temperature, so it was unknown whether gradual cooling would restore growth. It was also uncertain whether a 10 percent seed fraction was adequate, and whether it would hold at 6 C. It was unclear whether nitrite oxidizing bacteria were the bottleneck, since cold shock seemed to hit them harder than ammonia oxidizers.
sections.s244:
The technical uncertainty was whether nitrification start-up below 10 C could be shortened by preparing seed media before it entered cold water. Standard start-up took 9 to 10 weeks below 10 C, and warm seed media goes into shock in 8 C water. The company treated this as a separate question from its other cold-water biofilter work, so that each change could be linked to one result. The team tested whether stepwise acclimation of seed media shortens start-up, using three loops at 8 C. Each loop was a 1.2 m3 moving bed biofilter on the pilot RAS. Full nitrification was defined as processing 1 mg/L TAN to under 0.2 mg/L in 24 h. Nitrite also had to stay under 0.3 mg/L. Lab wet chemistry gave the reference for each reading.

It was hypothesized that if seed media is acclimated stepwise, then nitrification start-up at 8 C will take under 5 weeks. Acclimation drops temperature 1 C every 4 days from 14 C to 8 C, instead of moving seed straight into cold water. Unacclimated seed is expected to take longer, at 47 days. Any acclimated loop needing 35 days or more would disprove the hypothesis. [GAP: the reason for choosing 1 C every 4 days and the 14 C starting point was not given.]

The first question was whether warm seed alone would help at 8 C, given the shock seen in cold water. Loop A received no seed, only ammonium chloride dosing. Loop B had 10 percent of its media replaced with mature media from a 16 C production system, moved straight in. Loop A took 66 days to reach full nitrification and Loop B took 47 days. Seed therefore helped, but only partly, and the shock limited growth. This showed that the seed needed preparation before it could cut start-up much further.

The second question was whether stepwise acclimation would restore growth and shorten the stall at the nitrite stage. Loop C used the same 10 percent seed fraction as Loop B, but the seed was first held in a side tank and cooled 1 C every 4 days from 14 to 8 C. Loop C reached full nitrification in 31 days, against 47 days for unacclimated seed, which met the target of under 5 weeks. Loop B had stalled at the nitrite stage for 19 days, against 6 days for Loop C. Nitrite oxidizing bacteria seem to be hit harder by cold shock than ammonia oxidizers, which would make them the bottleneck. This is an inference from one stall observation, and the bacterial populations were not measured. [GAP: no replicate loops are described, so confidence in the single-loop results is unclear.]

The third question was whether the result would hold at 6 C and whether the 10 percent seed fraction was adequate. The team ran two loops at 6 C with acclimated seed at 5 and 15 percent. The 5 percent loop took 44 days, which missed the 5-week target. The 15 percent loop took 29 days, which met it. At 6 C more seed was therefore needed, and returns appeared to flatten above about 10 to 15 percent. [GAP: why the 5 percent loop missed the target was not examined.]

The objective was to understand cold-water nitrification start-up well enough to design RAS biofilters that start up in under 5 weeks at 8 C. That objective was met at 8 C: stepwise acclimation cut start-up to 31 days, against 47 days for unacclimated seed. The hypothesis was proven at 8 C. At 6 C, 5 percent acclimated seed took 44 days and missed the target, while 15 percent seed took 29 days and met it.

It was determined that warm seed media still helps at 8 C without acclimation, but only partly. Unacclimated seed took 47 days, against 66 days for the unseeded control. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether warm seed could grow in 8 C water. Warm seed dropped straight into cold water gave only a partial gain, so the shock limited growth. Acclimation was needed to cut start-up well below 47 days.

Through this investigation, it was established that stepwise acclimation restores growth in shocked seed media. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether gradual cooling from 14 to 8 C would shorten start-up. Loop B stalled at the nitrite stage for 19 days (almost three weeks), against 6 days for Loop C. Nitrite oxidizing bacteria seem to be the bottleneck, but this is an inference, since the bacterial populations were not measured. Each condition ran as a single loop, so replicate confidence is unknown.

Open work remains on whether the feed-forward rule needs to change with fish size. The seed fraction at 6 C also remains open below 15 percent, since only the 5 and 15 percent loops were run.

The knowledge gained answers the project goal of faster cold-water nitrification start-up. Stepwise acclimation of seed media cut start-up at 8 C to 31 days, against 47 days for unacclimated seed. This improved the biofilter start-up process for cold-water RAS designs.

sections.s242:
It was unclear whether sensor bias could be separated from real process change in a coupled dryer system, and this open question set the direction of the project. [GAP: confirm company name] is a company that builds controllers and analytics software for grain dryers. The company set out to build an early-warning feature that detects burner and grain-column faults before they become dangerous. Its controller reads temperature and moisture sensors and runs the burner and discharge rate on continuous-flow tower and mixed-flow dryers, which gave the team direct field experience of how sensor behaviour changes through a harvest season.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to give early warning of dryer faults was insufficient. Fixed-threshold alarms are late, because by the time plenum temperature crosses the threshold the fault is well along. Existing understanding of drift compensation did not cover this setting, as known methods assume a trusted reference sensor or periodic calibration, and the company has neither. Retraining on drifted data teaches a model that drift is normal, which can hide real slow faults, so no documented method separated sensor drift from slowly developing faults.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of how sensor bias can be separated from real process change in a coupled dryer system, for the purposes of providing burner and column fault warnings with a median lead time of at least 15 minutes and fewer than 0.25 false alarms per dryer-day under sensor drift of up to 3 °C per month.

It was unclear whether sensor bias could be separated from real process change in a coupled dryer system, because burner output, air flow, grain flow, ambient conditions and grain moisture all interact. It was uncertain whether online bias tracking could work with the sensors available, because known drift-compensation methods assume a trusted reference sensor or periodic calibration. Anything that makes a model more tolerant of slow change also makes it slower to see slow faults, so it was uncertain whether both targets could be held together. It was also uncertain whether the 11 documented faults were enough to validate any model.
sections.s244:
It was unclear whether sensor bias could be separated from real process change in a coupled dryer system, so the planned work tested that question in ordered phases. The team defined a false alarm as an alert with no fault within the next two hours, counted per dryer per day. Lead time runs from the alert to the earlier of the existing hard-limit alarm or the operator's manual shutdown. The team set both definitions in July 2025 before any run, so results could not be reinterpreted. The phases were a baseline rebuild under injected drift, synthetic drift training, an energy balance residual model with online bias tracking, and shadow mode trials on customer dryers in the fall 2025 harvest.

The hypothesis was that if anomaly scores use the energy balance residual (the plenum temperature expected from fuel rate, air flow and ambient temperature) with online bias tracking from redundant sensors, then false alarms stay below 0.25 per dryer-day under drift of up to 3 °C per month, with a median lead time of at least 15 minutes on burner and column faults.

Experiment one rebuilt the isolation forest baseline to measure how it fails under injected drift. The work also covered this: Billing portal migration to a new cloud host. In July and August 2025, the team trained the baseline on 2024 data from 14 dryers, about 11,000 dryer-hours. On held-out data with drift added, false alarms per dryer-day were 0.3 at zero drift, 1.4 at 2 °C per month by week four, and 2.6 at 3 °C per month. The baseline caught 9 of 11 real faults with a median lead time of 9 minutes. This confirmed the drift problem and showed that a different scoring basis was needed.

Experiment two trained on synthetic drift to see whether the model could ignore drift without losing fault detection. In August 2025, the team injected random slow drift into the training data, 0.5 to 3 °C per month on temperatures and up to 1.5 points per month on moisture. False alarms fell to 0.6 per dryer-day at 2 °C drift, but detection fell to 6 of 11 faults. It missed all three column plugs, which develop over 30 to 60 minutes, because the model had learned to treat slow rises as drift. The team dropped the approach.

Experiment three tested the energy balance residual with online bias tracking. In September 2025, the team fit a per-dryer energy balance on the first 48 hours of the season. A Kalman filter estimated a slow bias per sensor, limited to 4 °C per month, and updated only when the energy balance and redundant sensors agreed the process was steady. On 2024 data with 3 °C per month injected drift, false alarms were 0.18 per dryer-day, and 10 of 11 faults were caught, including all three column plugs, with a median lead time of 22 minutes. The one miss was an igniter fault on a single-sensor dryer, where the tracker could not separate drift from process change.

Experiment four ran in shadow mode on nine customer dryers from October 6 to November 21, 2025, with alerts logged but not shown to operators. Seven dryers had two plenum sensors and two had one. The dual-sensor dryers averaged 0.21 false alarms per dryer-day, with drift reaching 2.7 °C per month on one dryer, while the single-sensor dryers ran at 0.64. All four real events were flagged, with lead times of 14, 19, 26 and 31 minutes; the 14-minute flame event was under the 15-minute target.

Experiment five addressed the single-sensor dryers. From January to March 2026, the team used exhaust temperature as an indirect second reference for plenum bias and replayed the fall data. False alarms on those dryers dropped from 0.64 to 0.33 per dryer-day, still above the 0.25 target.
sections.s246:
It was unclear whether sensor bias could be separated from real process change in a coupled dryer system without a trusted reference sensor or recalibration. The objective was a median lead time of at least 15 minutes with fewer than 0.25 false alarms per dryer-day under sensor drift of up to 3 °C per month. Targets were met on injected drift: online bias tracking from redundant sensors, applied to the energy balance residual, gave 0.18 false alarms per dryer-day, 10 of 11 faults caught and a 22-minute median lead time. Single-sensor dryers missed the false alarm target (0.33 vs 0.25).

Through this investigation, it was established that training on synthetic drift hides slow faults, so it is not usable for separating sensor bias from process change. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether a model could ignore drift without ignoring slow real faults. Synthetic drift training cut false alarms to 0.6 per dryer-day but caught only 6 of 11 faults. Column plugs build over 30 to 60 minutes, and the model treated those slow rises as drift. Based on this understanding, the team dropped the approach and moved to the energy balance residual.

Single-sensor dryers remain above target, because the exhaust temperature fallback only cut false alarms from 0.64 to 0.33 per dryer-day. Flame event lead time was marginal, at 14 minutes on one event. Four real events occurred in the fall 2025 shadow mode trial, none in spring, so it remains unsettled whether the 11 documented faults suffice for validation. Alert performance with live operators is untested. A second field trial at the Ashgrove elevator is booked for spring 2027.

The goal was early burner and column fault warning that survives sensor drift without recalibration. The energy balance residual with online bias tracking met the target of fewer than 0.25 false alarms per dryer-day on injected drift, with a median lead time of 22 minutes against the 15-minute target. Dual-sensor dryers averaged 0.21 in shadow mode.

sections.s242:
Water-quality instrument maker Port Aldous is not a valid opener, so the section starts with the open question: it was unknown whether any window surface could resist biofilm for 30 days while staying optically clear at 254 nm, because coatings that resist fouling tend to absorb in the UV. The company designs and builds water-quality instruments for municipal treatment plants. It set out to build an in-line analyzer whose optical window stays accurate for at least 30 days without cleaning. Its optical analyzers measure UV absorbance at 254 nm as a proxy for dissolved organic carbon. A prior prototype with a fused silica window and mechanical wiper held calibration for only 14 days in secondary effluent.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to combine UV transparency, biofilm resistance and chemical durability in one window surface was insufficient. No published coating was UV-clear, food-grade safe, and durable in chlorinated water. Most fluoropolymers and hydrogels that resist fouling lose 30 to 60 percent of their transmission at 254 nm. Existing understanding of fouling correction assumed even attenuation across wavelengths. Biofilm contains its own organics that absorb in the UV, so a ratio correction had no established basis.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of UV-transparent anti-fouling window coatings and of dual-wavelength (254/365 nm) reference channel drift compensation, for the purposes of creating an in-line UV absorbance analyzer. It would hold drift under 5 percent raw, and within 2 percent corrected, for at least 30 days without cleaning.

It was uncertain whether a coating could keep at least 85 percent transmission at 254 nm when new and lose less than 5 percent over 30 days in secondary effluent. Chlorine and grit in the stream added doubt about whether it would survive. It was also uncertain whether fouling attenuation at 365 nm would track that at 254 nm closely enough to correct it, because the biofilm may change as it ages.
sections.s244:
The open question was whether any window surface could resist biofilm for 30 days while staying optically clear at 254 nm. The company's planned approach targeted it directly. The team planned coupon screening of four coatings against uncoated controls to test whether any window surface resists biofilm. The work ran from August to October 2025 in a secondary effluent side stream. Transmission at 254 nm was measured every 3 days. Fused silica coupons carried a fluorosilane monolayer, a silica sol-gel with a fluorinated top, a zwitterionic polymer brush or a thin titania film, with 12 coupons per candidate and 12 uncoated controls.

If a silica sol-gel has a fluorinated top surface, then raw drift stays under 5 percent for 30 days. The hypothesis fails if the coated window passes 5 percent loss in transmission before day 30 in secondary effluent, or if initial transmission at 254 nm falls below the 85 percent target.

The first uncertainty was which coating could combine UV clarity with biofilm resistance. The 42-day screening gave uncoated controls 5 percent loss by day 11 and 22 percent by day 42. The zwitterionic brush resisted biofilm best but transmitted only 71 percent initially. Titania grew film faster than the controls; the suspected cause, untested, is that in-stream UV is too low to activate it and that its rough surface aids attachment. The fluorosilane monolayer started at 92 percent and reached 5 percent loss by day 17. The sol-gel with fluorinated top started at 89 percent and took 31 days to lose 5 percent. Only the sol-gel met both targets, though the margin was narrow.

The next uncertainty was why fouling on the sol-gel coupons began at the edges, where the coating was thinnest, and whether layer evenness limited biofilm resistance. The team changed the dip withdrawal speed from 2 millimetres per second to 1 millimetre per second. The slower withdrawal gave a more even sol-gel layer of about 180 nanometres. The second coupon round reached 5 percent loss at day 38 with initial transmission of 87 percent. Initial transmission fell slightly from 89 percent but stayed above the 85 percent target. A more even layer therefore extended fouling resistance by 7 days while the clarity target was still met.

The remaining uncertainty was whether the coating would perform in plant conditions. Four complete Orion-2 units with coated windows ran at the Harbourside plant from February 9 to June 12 2026, two on secondary effluent and two on chlorinated final effluent. Grab samples taken twice a week and analyzed on a lab spectrophotometer served as the reference. On secondary effluent, raw drift crossed 5 percent at day 36 and day 40. On final effluent, drift was lower, but one unit lost 9 percent of its transmission between day 70 and day 90, a loss not attributed to biofilm. The team suspects chlorine is slowly attacking the fluorinated layer, but this was not confirmed. Coating durability in chlorinated water beyond about 70 days remains unresolved.
sections.s246:
Whether a window surface could resist biofilm for 30 days and stay optically clear at 254 nm was the open question, and the coating side of the objective was met in part. A sol-gel with a fluorinated top met both coating targets, with 87 percent initial transmission and 5 percent loss at day 38 in the second coupon round. In the field, raw drift crossed 5 percent at day 36 and day 40. Durability in chlorinated water was not established, and the dual-wavelength correction lies outside this coating-focused advancement.

Through this investigation, it was determined that a sol-gel with a fluorinated top can combine UV clarity with biofilm resistance, though the first round met both targets just barely. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether any window surface could resist biofilm for 30 days while staying optically clear at 254 nm. Fouling started at the edges where the coating was thinnest, so layer evenness affects biofilm resistance. Based on this understanding, the team slowed the dip withdrawal from 2 to 1 millimetre per second. The slower withdrawal gave a more even layer of about 180 nanometres.

Coating durability in chlorinated water beyond 70 days is unresolved. One final effluent unit lost 9 percent of its transmission between day 70 and day 90, a loss not attributed to biofilm. The team suspects chlorine attacks the fluorinated layer, but this was not confirmed. Fiscal 2027 work will address this open question.

The team sought a UV-clear window coating that resists biofilm, and a sol-gel with a fluorinated top met both targets. The earlier fused silica window with a mechanical wiper held calibration for only 14 days in secondary effluent, so the coating moves the analyzer toward the 30-day goal without cleaning.

sections.s242:
It was uncertain whether burr height could be estimated from fast 2D images accurately enough, and quickly enough, to set deburring force for each edge of a cast A357 aluminium bracket. The team sought to learn whether the estimate could meet both limits for per-edge force. The company designs and builds robotic finishing cells, including grinding, sanding, polishing and deburring, mostly for aerospace and some medical parts. It set out to build a deburring cell for brackets of about 180 x 90 mm that holds a consistent rounded edge within a 4-minute cycle.

Standard practice lacked the knowledge to set deburring force from the burr on each edge. A fixed-force cell either over-rounds small burrs or leaves large ones when burr height varies from 0.1 to 1.2 mm. No documented method estimated burr height on cast aluminium from fast 2D images, because the surface is shiny in places and dull in others and the burr is small relative to the part. A full scan of one bracket takes about 90 seconds, too long for a 4-minute cycle, and touch probing was also too slow. No model linked burr height, compliant spindle force and edge radius, and thin 2.5 mm flanges flex under load.

The technological objective was to advance understanding of 2D vision-based burr height estimation and of the relationship between burr height and compliant spindle force on cast A357 aluminium, in order to create an adaptive cell that holds an edge radius of 0.2 to 0.5 mm within a 4-minute cycle.

It was uncertain whether burr height per edge could be estimated from 2D images to within 0.1 mm RMS. The same estimate also had to finish in under 120 ms per edge. Image appearance depends on lighting angle and burr shape, and reflections from machined faces can mimic burr signal. It was uncertain whether per-edge force could hold an edge radius of 0.2 to 0.5 millimetres on every edge, because casting variation, thin-flange flex and chatter at higher forces could make the force-to-radius relationship too unstable to control.
sections.s244:
The technical uncertainty was whether burr height per edge could be estimated from 2D images to within 0.1 mm RMS in under 120 ms, and whether per-edge force could then hold the edge radius window. The team planned to test this in the Bay 4 pilot cell using customer A357 brackets. The steps ran in order: a fixed-force baseline, a 2D estimate checked against a laser profiler, a burr-height-to-force map tested on real brackets, then longer trials for casting variation and abrasive wear. In August 2025 the team first checked that the modified compliant spindle could change force between edges, which it did in about 80 ms.

It was hypothesized that if burr height per edge is estimated from 2D images to within 0.1 mm RMS in under 120 ms, and that estimate sets compliant spindle force for each edge, then at least 97 percent of edges will fall within the edge radius window of 0.2 to 0.5 mm and rejects will fall below 3 percent.

The first question was the cost of fixed force. The company ran 120 brackets at a fixed 20 N on a fixed path. Cycle time was 3:10 and rejects were 14 percent. About two thirds of rejects were leftover burrs on high-burr edges, and the rest were edges over-rounded above 0.5 mm. Fixed force therefore performed worse than the customer's hand deburring, which confirmed that force had to follow the burr on each edge.

The next question was whether one camera could estimate burr height. The company used a 12 MP camera with a low-angle ring light on 400 edges, referenced to a laser profiler. Single-angle imaging gave 0.18 mm RMS at about 210 ms per edge, missing both limits. Reflections on machined faces made some burrs look much taller; 31 of 400 edges were overestimated by more than 0.4 mm, all on machined faces. A single-angle setup could not separate burr signal from reflection.

The company then tested whether depth sensing would avoid the problem. It borrowed a structured light 3D camera for two weeks. Depth resolution was about 0.2 mm at working distance, with about 400 ms per capture. That was no better than the 2D result on accuracy and slower on speed, so the team returned to 2D.

The team revised the 2D method. It took two shots per edge at 15 and 60 degrees and applied two-angle differencing, because burr shadow changes with lighting angle differently from reflection off a flat face. GPU processing and cropping to a region around each edge from the CAD path addressed speed. On the same 400 edges, error fell to 0.07 mm RMS at 95 ms per edge, with a worst single-edge error of 0.19 mm. Both targets were met.

The company then mapped force to radius using 60 coupons cut from scrap brackets, with burrs of 0.1 to 1.2 mm and forces of 8 to 40 N. The relationship was non-linear, rising from about 10 N to 22 N for burrs up to about 0.6 mm, then steeper to about 34 N at 1.2 mm. A lookup table run on 300 brackets gave 4.3 percent rejects, 96.1 percent of edges in the window and a 3:50 cycle. Most rejects were on 2.5 mm thin flanges, where above about 28 N the flange flexed and the head chattered. Thin flanges therefore limited usable force.

Test 5 capped force at 26 N on thin flanges and cut feed from 40 to 25 mm/s, on 360 brackets from casting lots 2 and 3. A second pass on 40 brackets gave 3.9 percent rejects, so slower feed worked better. In this single run, chatter stopped, rejects were 2.6 percent, 97.8 percent of edges were in the window and cycle time was 3:58. Last, a reference coupon deburred and imaged every 25 brackets scaled the force map. Without correction, radius drifted smaller over about 150 brackets. Over 240 brackets the reject rate stayed at 2.4 percent, with no drift trend across the run.
sections.s246:
It was uncertain whether burr height per edge could be estimated from 2D images to within 0.1 mm RMS in under 120 ms. Two-angle imaging resolved it: error fell to 0.07 mm RMS at 95 ms per edge, which met both targets. The hypothesis was therefore proven for the estimate. Its second half, that per-edge force holds the edge radius window, was not proven in the first force map run: 96.1 percent of edges fell in the window against the 97 percent target, because thin flanges chattered above about 28 N.

It was determined that two lighting angles with two-angle differencing separate burr shadow from surface reflection, because the shadow changes with angle differently from reflection off a flat face. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether 2D imaging could meet the accuracy and speed limits. A single-angle camera with a low-angle ring light could not: it gave 0.18 mm RMS at about 210 ms per edge, and reflections on machined faces overstated some burrs. A borrowed 3D camera, with about 0.2 mm depth resolution, was no better, so the team returned to 2D. Based on this understanding, the company set per-edge force from the two-angle estimate.

It remains untested whether burr height can be estimated on internal edges the camera cannot view straight on. The uncertainty persists because a straight-on view is what the two-angle method relies on, and these edges do not allow one. Transfer to other alloys and bracket designs, and any further cut in GPU time, are also unresolved.

The goal was a deburring cell that holds an edge radius of 0.2 to 0.5 mm within a 4-minute cycle on cast A357 brackets. The team learned that burr height could be estimated from 2D images to 0.07 mm RMS at 95 ms per edge. That estimate now drives per-edge compliant spindle force in the pilot cell, replacing the fixed force that gave 14 percent rejects.

A writer uploaded a detailed PD Writing Customized Settings document before the first draft, chat listed 16 places where the draft deviated, and the second draft still deviated after a bulk revision. The settings document is uploaded as Writer's Notes (category writer_notes) by the reviewer account the suite acts as. The scripted writer makes no decision of its own: the first Seed on each step, approve, sign off. Previous-year status is skipped because the project started in July 2025. So the fixture measures the settings document, not the writer's choices.

Review fixes (2026-10-02, lead review, Claude Opus 5.5): one matcher for every term, synonym, banned phrase and exclusion marker. It matches whole words in any case, a space or a hyphen between words, and the last word singular or with s or es, so "DFTs", "substrate temperatures", "edge-wrap" and "dry-film thickness" are breaks and "outgassing defect rate" uses "outgassing defects". Every scored synonym is one the settings document names.

The settings document says never to write pinholes, pinholing, blisters or blistering on their own, so one of them in a sentence that also says outgassing defects is not a break (allowedWithTerm). A banned word counts only in the forms listed: "break-through" is the MEK test term ("no break-through to the board"), not "breakthrough", and "successful" and "unsuccessfully" are not counted as forms of "successfully". The judges decide whether such a word breaks the rule.

project.title: Release eval - Velloway low-temperature powder on MDF

sections.s242:
The company is a contract finisher of MDF panels, including cabinet doors and display panels for other companies. The company set out to offer a solvent-free powder finish on thick routed doors. Two of its biggest customers said in 2024 they would move to a powder finisher. The company had run no powder panels before July 2025.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to powder coat 25 mm routed MDF was insufficient, as powder processes on MDF existed only for thin flat panels, which is what suppliers show. No documented methods or published data gave the panel surface temperature at which outgassing defects begin on thick routed board, or how charge shielding behaves in a concave cove.

The aim of this work was to powder coat 25 mm routed MDF doors at 2.5 metres per minute, advancing the understanding of how to separate surface conductivity from heat and reach full cure below the outgassing onset.

It was not known at the outset whether conductivity could be reached without preheat that causes outgassing defects, because the moisture that makes MDF conductive is the same moisture that leaves the board during cure. Outgassing defects began at a panel surface temperature of about 118 to 122 C, which left little room for full cure and a usable cure window.
sections.s244:
The team planned a staged investigation around one conflict: making MDF conductive enough for powder to stick and curing the powder both need heat, and heat drives gas out of the board. Targets were 70 to 90 microns film build on faces, edge coverage of at least 60 microns, at most 1 outgassing defect per square metre, 50 MEK double rubs, cure at 120 C or less, a cure window at least 8 C wide, and 2.5 metres per minute. The team logged surface temperature with thermocouples on every test panel and changed one thing at a time.

It was hypothesized that if an edge sealer replaces preheat, then edge coverage will reach 60 microns with outgassing defects at most 1 per square metre.

Trial 1 followed the supplier datasheet on 25 mm routed MDF: IR preheat to 110 C, a standard low-temperature powder and a convection oven at 135 C air for 10 minutes. The datasheet process reached 131 C, with 14 outgassing defects per square metre overall and 30 on routed edges. Edge film build was 35 microns against 82 on faces, and MEK rubs were 55 to 62.

Trial 2 lowered oven air to 125 C and extended dwell from 10 to 14 minutes, then tried 127 C with several dwell times. At 125 C air, the panel surface temperature peaked at 121 C and defects fell to 4 per square metre, but MEK rubs dropped to 30, so the powder was undercured. Outgassing onset, at about 118 to 122 C, did not move with dwell time, and cure was lost below about 122 C. The team concluded that peak panel surface temperature, not dwell time, controlled outgassing defects.

Trial 3 applied a water-based conductive edge sealer to routed edges only, flash-dried it for 6 minutes at 60 C, and cut preheat from 110 C to 85 C. Edge film build averaged 58 microns with 1.8 outgassing defects per square metre. Overspray reduced face adhesion to 3B against a 5B target on 12 percent of panels; an edge-only nozzle and face mask restored 5B.

Trial 4 tested a fast-catalysed polyester-epoxy hybrid with the supplier. The fastest catalyst level gave full cure at 120 C in 9 minutes, with a cure window of 113 to 121 C. Orange peel 5 fell short of the target of 6. On 140 panels, edge film build averaged 64 microns with 0.6 outgassing defects per square metre.

Trial 5 ran 600 doors at 2.5 metres per minute. Shaker edges met 60 microns on all 420 panels, at 0.8 outgassing defects per square metre. On 180 deep cove profile panels, 13 percent fell below 60 microns. MEK failures came from one batch on the day oven zone 3 drifted 6 C low.
sections.s246:
The aim was to separate surface conductivity from heat and reach full cure below the outgassing onset on 25 mm routed MDF. This was partly achieved. Outgassing defects started at a panel surface temperature of about 118 to 122 C, whatever the dwell time, so peak temperature, not time, sets the ceiling. Shaker doors met the targets; the deep cove profile did not.

The datasheet process for flat panels failed on 25 mm routed MDF. Trial 1 reached 131 C with 14 outgassing defects per square metre, and defects tracked peak panel surface temperature, not dwell time. This explained why the supplier process left no usable cure window under the ceiling of about 118 to 122 C. The team cut preheat from 110 C to 85 C using an edge sealer and moved to a fast-catalysed powder that cured fully at 120 C, with a cure window of 113 to 121 C.

The shaker doors are ready for production, but the deep cove profile is not. On 180 deep cove panels, 13 percent fell below 60 microns edge coverage. It is unknown whether a different edge sealer, gun angle or cove geometry can raise it, because charge shielding in the concave cove has not been quantified. Oven zone control also remains open, since a 6 C drift falls outside an 8 C cure window. Further trials are planned for fiscal 2027.

The project goal was a solvent-free powder finish on 25 mm routed doors at 2.5 metres per minute. Shaker doors reached it in the pilot.
